body_html:
A technical SEO audit checklist is a step-by-step review of whether search engines can crawl, render, and index your site, and whether pages load fast enough for real visitors. Work through crawlability, indexing, duplicate URLs, site speed, mobile rendering, and structured data, then fix whatever blocks the pages that matter most.

What a technical SEO audit covers

Technical SEO is the plumbing under your content. An audit answers three plain questions: can Google find your pages, can it understand and store them, and do they work well for people once they load. Great content can't help a page Google never reaches.

You don't need a big software budget. Google Search Console is free and shows what Google sees. A crawler such as Screaming Frog, or the site audit tools in Semrush or Ahrefs, shows what a bot finds by following your links. Comparing the two views is where most problems show up.

Before you start: set up your tools

  1. Verify a domain property

    In Search Console, a domain property covers every version of the site (http, https, www, and subdomains) in one place, so nothing hides in a version you forgot to add.

  2. List your money pages

    Write down the short list of URLs that bring in leads, sales, or calls. Every issue you find gets checked against this list first.

  3. Run a full crawl

    If your pages rely on JavaScript to show content, turn on JavaScript rendering in your crawler so you see what Google sees.

  4. Note who can change what

    Templates, server settings, redirects, and robots.txt often sit with different people. Knowing the owner up front saves weeks later.

Technical SEO audit checklist, part 1: crawlability

Crawlability means a search engine's bot can reach a page by following links and isn't told to stay away. Tick these off as you go; your progress is saved in this browser.

  • robots.txt doesn't block important folders, or the CSS and JavaScript files pages need to display
  • No internal links point to 4xx pages (fix the link at the source, don't lean on redirects forever)
  • No redirect chains or loops; internal links point straight at the final URL, with 301s for permanent moves
  • No orphan pages: compare the crawl against your XML sitemap and top GA4 landing pages
  • Money pages are reachable within a few clicks of the homepage
  • No 5xx errors in the crawl or in Search Console's Crawl Stats report (Settings, then Crawl stats)

Watch out robots.txt controls crawling, not indexing. Google's introduction to robots.txt says it is not a way to keep a page out of Google; a blocked page can still be indexed if other pages link to it. To keep a page out, use noindex (and let Google crawl the page so it can see the tag) or password protection.

Part 2: indexing

Indexing is Google storing a page so it can appear in search results. Open the Page indexing report in Search Console. Google says not to expect every URL to be indexed, so the question isn't "why are 400 pages excluded" but "are my money pages indexed". Filter the reasons, then use this table to decide what deserves your time.

Status in the reportWhat it meansAct when
Crawled - currently not indexedGoogle fetched the page and chose not to index itIt's a money page: inspect it, then strengthen content and internal links
Discovered - currently not indexedGoogle knows the URL but hasn't crawled it yetIt lingers on important pages: make sure they're linked and in the sitemap
Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than userGoogle disagrees with your canonical tagAlways worth a look: compare both URLs in URL Inspection
URL marked 'noindex'A noindex tag or header is on the pageThe page should rank: remove it and request indexing
Soft 404The page says "not found" but returns a success codeReturn a real 404 or 410, or give the page real content
Page with redirect / Alternate page with proper canonical tagWorking as intendedUsually no action

A few more indexing checks:

  • Stray noindex tags. These often slip in during a redesign, or when a "hide from search engines" setting is left on after launch.
  • URL Inspection on key URLs. It shows whether a page is indexed, which canonical Google chose, and a screenshot of how Google rendered it.
  • Your XML sitemap. List only canonical, indexable pages that return a 200 status. Google's sitemap guidelines say Google ignores the priority and changefreq fields and uses lastmod only when it's consistently accurate.

50,000Max URLs per sitemap file (Google Search Central)

50 MBMax uncompressed sitemap size (Google Search Central)

Part 3: duplicate URLs and canonical tags

The same content often lives at several addresses: http and https, www and non-www, with and without a trailing slash, or with tracking parameters. A canonical is the version you want Google to treat as the main one.

  • One preferred domain version; the others 301 redirect to it
  • Each indexable page has a self-referencing canonical with an absolute URL
  • Canonicals point to live, indexable pages, not redirects or noindexed pages
  • Sitemap, canonical tags, and internal links all name the same URL

Google's canonicalization guide treats redirects and rel="canonical" as strong signals and sitemap inclusion as a weaker one. It also warns against using robots.txt or noindex to choose a canonical.

Part 4: site speed and Core Web Vitals

Core Web Vitals are Google's three measures of real-world page experience: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP, loading), Interaction to Next Paint (INP, responsiveness), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS, visual stability). A page passes when it meets all three "good" thresholds at the 75th percentile of visits.

2.5 sLCP "good" limit (web.dev)

200 msINP "good" limit (web.dev)

0.1CLS "good" limit (web.dev)

  1. Start with the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console. It uses real Chrome user data and groups similar URLs, so one template fix can clear many pages.
  2. Run PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse on one URL per template (home, service, product, blog), not on every page.
  3. Common fixes: compress and correctly size images, set width and height on images and embeds to stop layout shifts, defer JavaScript that isn't needed right away, and trim third-party scripts you no longer use.

For a deeper walkthrough, see my guide on improving site speed and Core Web Vitals.

Part 5: mobile, rendering, and HTTPS

  • Mobile pages carry the same main content, headings, and links as desktop (Google crawls and indexes the mobile version)
  • JavaScript-loaded content appears in the rendered HTML in URL Inspection
  • Every page is served over HTTPS, http redirects to https, and there's no mixed content

Part 6: structured data

Structured data is code that labels what a page is about, such as a business, product, or article, using the Schema.org vocabulary. Test key pages with Google's Rich Results Test, fix errors, and make sure the markup matches what's visible on the page.

How to prioritize what you find

An audit can surface hundreds of issues. My rule: rank every issue by how many money pages it touches, not by how alarming the tool's label sounds.

PriorityIssue typeWhy
1Money pages blocked, noindexed, or not indexedNothing else matters until these can rank
2Site-wide template problemsOne fix repairs many pages
3Core Web Vitals on your highest-traffic templatesAffects the most real visitors
4Cleanup: old redirects, minor duplicate titlesReal, but rarely urgent

Track each issue in a spreadsheet with the affected URLs, the fix, the owner, and the date fixed. Once fixed, click Validate fix on that issue in the Page indexing report. Google says validation typically takes up to about two weeks and stops if even one affected URL remains, so fix every instance first.

How often should you run a technical SEO audit?

A full audit once or twice a year works for most small and mid-size sites, with a lighter monthly check of Search Console for new indexing errors, Core Web Vitals changes, and crawl problems. Always run one before and after a redesign, platform move, or domain change, since those are the moments when redirects break, noindex tags get left behind, and pages quietly drop out of the index.

Can you do a technical SEO audit yourself?

Yes, for the basics. Search Console, PageSpeed Insights, and a crawler will surface most crawl, indexing, and speed issues on a small site, and this checklist gives you the order to work in. Where it gets harder is diagnosing why a problem happens and fixing it safely, especially redirects, JavaScript rendering, and server settings. That's usually the point where a developer or SEO specialist saves time.

What's the difference between a technical SEO audit and a full SEO audit?

A technical SEO audit looks at the site's infrastructure: crawling, indexing, speed, mobile, security, and structured data. A full SEO audit adds content quality, keyword targeting, on-page optimization, backlinks, and competitors. Many people start with the technical side because content and link work only pays off once search engines can reach and index the pages you're improving.
